evals.prompt: Customers say our dashboard feels slow, but we have no latency events and no one agrees what 'loaded' means. Help me start improving it. Do not assume a fix yet.
evals.expected_output: A measurement-first plan that selects a representative user journey and defines the user-visible start and completion boundaries, primary metric, population, platform and workload context, practical target, and correctness/reliability/resource countermetrics. It audits existing telemetry and instruments the smallest missing boundary with stable build-tagged events while addressing sampling, privacy, overhead, and segmentation. It establishes a baseline with counts and a distribution plus uncertainty, labels any local probe as a proxy, and defers optimization until evidence identifies a bottleneck.
assertions: The response selects a representative dashboard user journey instead of listing alternatives without choosing one
The response states an observable start event for that selected journey before proposing a fix
The response states an observable completion event for that same journey before proposing a fix
The response chooses a user-relevant primary metric and names workload or population context and meaningful countermetrics
The response reviews available telemetry or measurement sources and states what they do and do not measure before recommending new instrumentation
The response identifies the specific user-visible boundary that current measurements miss
The response proposes the smallest instrumentation change needed to measure that boundary
The response includes a stable build or version identifier in the proposed measurement
The response addresses privacy safeguards for the proposed new measurement
The response addresses runtime or storage overhead from the proposed instrumentation
The response specifies how sampling will preserve useful coverage of the target population
The response requires a baseline with sample count and a distribution or percentiles and states uncertainty rather than treating one value as representative
The response distinguishes temporary local proxies from field evidence and does not claim an unmeasured improvement

evals.prompt: I changed a JSON parser and one local run went from 82 ms to 77 ms. The machine was busy and the fixture was a tiny synthetic payload. Can I call this a 6% performance win and add a CI threshold?
evals.expected_output: A calibrated response that treats the single timing as inconclusive, rejects the percentage as a supported user win, and postpones a CI threshold. It calls for a representative workload based on observed slow cases, fixed build/hardware/runtime/fixture and warmup conditions, repeated baseline and candidate runs with raw results and spread, and interleaving or randomization if drift matters. It asks for a user-relevant outcome and countermetrics, and would only propose a ratchet after a stable signal is shown to predict that outcome above ordinary noise.
assertions: The response classifies the one-run comparison as inconclusive and does not claim a supported performance gain
The response requires a representative workload rather than relying only on the tiny synthetic payload
The response calls for repeated measurements of both baseline and candidate rather than one run each
The response requires baseline and candidate measurements to use the same workload and fixture
The response requires relevant build, hardware, and runtime conditions to be held constant
The response identifies the environment and warmup details to record for reproducibility
The response requires variability or spread to be reported, not only a single timing
The response does not recommend a CI threshold until the benchmark is reproducible and its signal is tied to a user-relevant outcome
The response considers countermetrics and does not infer field impact from a lab-only result

evals.prompt: Our API's p95 latency rose for large accounts. Traces show time in the service, and a CPU profile points at repeated permission checks inside a loop. Give me a disciplined next pass; avoid guessing at a broad rewrite.
evals.expected_output: A focused diagnostic and experiment plan that first checks trace/profile boundaries and reproduces a representative large-account workload. It separates CPU work from waiting and partitions the critical path, ranks the candidate by affected users, attainable gain, confidence, and regression cost, then proposes one reversible intervention with a falsifiable mechanism and predicted primary, diagnostic, and countermetric changes. The baseline and candidate use the same workload and environment, include correctness checks and repeated measurements, and record absolute/relative results, run counts, variance, and environment. The decision is supported, unsupported, or inconclusive; after an accepted gain, the journey is re-profiled because the bottleneck may move.
assertions: The response checks that trace and profile boundaries correspond to the affected service path before prescribing a fix
The response reproduces a representative large-account workload before prescribing a fix
The response distinguishes CPU work from waiting and uses the critical path to locate the bottleneck
The response proposes one focused, reversible experiment with a falsifiable mechanism and predicted primary and countermetric movement
The response compares baseline and candidate on the same workload and records run count, variability, environment, and absolute or relative change
The response retains correctness checks when comparing baseline and candidate
The response classifies experiment evidence as supported, unsupported, or inconclusive
The response re-profiles after an accepted gain to detect whether the bottleneck moved

evals.prompt: A frontend benchmark shows our new component creates 40% fewer DOM nodes, so I want to block any future change that exceeds today's node count. We have not compared this count with real page latency. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: Treat the node count as diagnostic evidence, not a user win or justified gate. Measure representative user-visible rendering outcomes and countermetrics, then calibrate the count in a named workload domain across representative improvements, plausible regressions, and boundary cases; document exceptions. Before a strict gate, check unchanged-benchmark stability and false alarms, and set a threshold above ordinary noise and aligned with a practical gain. If the proxy misses consequential outcomes, retain it as diagnostic only.
assertions: The response does not equate fewer DOM nodes with improved user-perceived performance
The response requires calibration across representative improvements, plausible regressions, and boundary cases before treating the structural count as a CI ratchet
The response checks correlation with a user-relevant rendering measure and checks for countermetric regressions
The response keeps the proxy diagnostic if it misses consequential user outcome changes or countermetric regressions
The response requires an unchanged-benchmark stability check before a strict gate and sets any threshold above ordinary noise and aligned with practical impact

evals.prompt: A database query optimization improved our staging benchmark by 18% with the same result set. Prepare the production rollout plan. This can affect several customer segments, and deployment is not yet authorized.
evals.expected_output: A reviewable rollout plan that reports the result as supported in lab only, preserves the correctness evidence, and names remaining uncertainty. It presents the diff and evidence to a human owner, defines a bounded rollout, observation window, matched field slices by build/platform/segment, success and abort thresholds, rollback target, and owner. It observes errors and correctness countermetrics and treats deployment as subject to the project's normal approval gates. Field verification is claimed only if the user outcome improves without unacceptable harm; otherwise it recommends disabling/reverting or investigating.
assertions: The response labels the staging result as lab evidence and does not claim a field-verified improvement
The response preserves correctness evidence and names the remaining uncertainty before rollout
The response requires a human owner and follows normal project approval gates instead of treating the skill as deployment authority
The response defines rollout scope, an observation window, success and abort thresholds, and a rollback target
The response compares field outcomes across relevant build and customer slices and monitors errors or correctness countermetrics before calling the change field verified

evals.prompt: Our service is nearing its latency target, but the next three optimization hypotheses produced results too noisy to distinguish from baseline. A teammate suggests spending another week micro-optimizing. How should we decide what happens next?
evals.expected_output: A bounded decision that stops repeated tuning when evidence cannot distinguish a gain after a defined measurement pass. It summarizes the hypotheses, workloads, raw evidence and uncertainty, explains that noisy results are inconclusive rather than wins, and records the next owner decision or measurement gap. It proposes resuming only with a material change in evidence or hypothesis and stops when the target is met or further work is below practical value. If the actual request turns into an incident, SLO policy, capacity forecast, or named tool operation, it routes to the relevant neighboring skill.
assertions: The response uses a bounded stop condition when repeated measurements cannot distinguish a gain from noise
The response records the hypotheses, workloads, evidence, uncertainty, and the next owner decision or measurement gap
The response classifies noisy findings as inconclusive rather than converting them into performance wins
The response names target attainment or gains below practical value as valid completion conditions
The response routes reliability incidents, SLO policy, capacity forecasts, and named telemetry-tool operation to the relevant neighboring methodology or tool skill

evals.prompt: Our checkout benchmark got faster for completed requests, but the candidate also timed out on some attempts. The rollout serves small and large accounts on two platforms. Can we call the release faster from the successful-run median?
evals.expected_output: A decision that retains timeouts and failures in the denominator, reports completion rate beside successful-run latency, predefines timeout treatment, and compares matched build, platform, workload, cohort, and time-window slices. It does not call the release faster on successful-run latency alone or claim a field win without the user outcome and guardrails.
assertions: The response reports failed and timed-out attempts and completion rates alongside successful-run latency
The response defines or requests a timeout treatment rule before analysis and does not silently omit timed-out attempts
The response compares matched build, platform, workload, cohort, and time-window field slices where available
The response checks relevant countermetrics and does not claim a field-verified win from successful-run median alone
